Let’s talk about something that really matters on this journey— practicing self-compassion and sustaining the process.
You know, keeping nonviolent communication alive in your daily life isn’t about being perfect all the time.
Old habits—like judging yourself, blaming, or getting stuck in self-criticism—can sneak back in, especially when you’re stressed out. But here’s the thing: it’s not about never messing up. It’s about coming back, again and again, to your intention—choosing understanding and connection over harshness.
So, what does self-compassion really look like? Well, it’s basically nonviolent communication turned inward.
When you catch yourself in a loop of harsh self-talk or feeling like you’re falling short, try this: pause for a moment.
Notice what’s happening, name what you’re feeling, connect with the need underneath, and then make a gentle, kind request of yourself.
Let’s say you just finished a tough conversation and your first thought is, “Ugh, I handled that so badly.” Instead of letting that spiral into self-criticism, you might try saying, “I notice I’m feeling regret because I really want to contribute to harmony. I’d like to take a moment to care for myself—and maybe think about how I could approach things differently next time.”
Simple, right? But it takes practice. Here are a few ways to weave self-compassion into your day:
First, daily check-ins. Just give yourself a few minutes each day to notice your feelings and needs—no judgment, just gentle curiosity.
Second, try journaling. Write about those tough moments, and walk yourself through the four steps: observation, feeling, need, and request. It helps you see your experience more clearly.
And don’t forget to celebrate your progress. Seriously—acknowledge those times, even the small ones, when you managed to respond with empathy. It all adds up.
Keeping this approach going also means reaching out for support. Practice with a friend, join a study group, or find a mentor who gets what you’re trying to do.
Over time, these little practices start to feel natural. They shape not just the words you use, but the way you show up in the world.
This path—this way of communicating—it’s a journey, not a finish line. Every conversation is a chance to learn, to heal, and to build bridges of understanding.
So, whenever you feel lost, just come back to the basics: observe what’s going on, notice your feelings, connect with your needs, and make a kind request.
That’s how you lay the groundwork for relationships that are honest, resilient, and deeply human.
